summary: Silver Oak Capital's /private-bank-mortgages/ page (search-result title 'Private Bank Mortgages UK') presents a private bank mortgage as a bespoke form of real estate finance offered by private banks to their high net worth clients, where the existing client-bank relationship lets lenders go far beyond standing lending criteria; it is positioned for clients with complex finances, large borrowing needs or unusual ownership structures. Supporting pages (FAQ, /types-of-borrowing/, /prime-london-mortgages/) add that private banks have very flexible underwriting criteria and can make very large loans with no fixed cap, that such mortgages suit any HNWI, international or local, can be tailored regardless of loan structure, can be interest-only or capitalising, and that lending policy varies by the bank branch approving the loan. The page body itself was only partially surfaced (3 summarized sentences via query b); no rates, LTVs, fees, minimum sizes, process steps or testimonials specific to this page were revealed. Silver Oak is a broker, not a bank.

sections.heading: What is a private bank mortgage (target page, as summarized by search [b])
sections.content: A private bank mortgage is described as a bespoke form of real estate finance offered by private banks to their high net worth clients. The existing relationship between the client and the bank lets lenders go far beyond standing lending criteria.

sections.heading: Who it suits (target page, as summarized by search [b])
sections.content: These loans fit clients with complex finances, large borrowing needs, or unusual ownership structures.

sections.heading: Related FAQ content on private bank mortgages (/faq/ [a][b])
sections.content: Private banks have very flexible underwriting criteria and can therefore make very large loans; there is no fixed cap on borrowing. Private bank mortgages are suitable for any HNWI, international or local. They can be tailored to suit the needs of the borrower regardless of the structure of the loan, and can be interest-only or capitalising.
